# Meet the Students {#sec-meet-students .unnumbered}

<!-- Status: FIRST DRAFT (2026-10-18). Characters per docs/characters.md (decision D11). Pending the author's voice edit. -->

Before the first chapter, meet five people you will see again and again in this book. They are students in an "AI for All" course, much like the one you may be taking. They are also **fictional**. The section after their story explains why they are here and how to read them.

## Thursday, Week 1 {.unnumbered}

The lab room smelled of new carpet and old coffee. Five students who had never met found their names printed on a card at the same table.

**Lucía Herrera** arrived first, straight from a morning shift answering customer chats for a software company. She opened a laptop with a cracked corner and a paper planner full of color codes. "I use AI every day," she said to no one in particular. "It writes half my replies at work. I'm here to get faster."

**Marcus Bell** sat down across from her and did not open anything. He had spent three years as a nursing assistant before starting his nursing degree. "Last year a patient showed me an answer a chatbot gave her about her medication," he said. "It was confident, and it was wrong. So I'm here to find out why anyone trusts these things."

**Elif Kaya** had been in the country for eleven days. She had flown in from İzmir, and English was her second language. She carried a notebook with Turkish words on the left and English words on the right. "I use AI to check my English," she said carefully. "But I am not sure if that is allowed. And sometimes my sentences come back sounding like somebody else."

**Sam Okafor** dropped his backpack, which had a robotics club patch on it, and grinned. He was a senior in mechanical engineering and had just finished a co-op term at a manufacturing plant. "I want to automate everything," he said. "If a computer can do it, why should I?"

**Hana Nguyen** came in last, sketchbook under one arm. They studied media arts and design and paid part of their tuition with freelance illustration for local shops. They sat down and said quietly, "I'm here because I'm worried. These image tools learned from artists like me, and nobody asked us."

For a moment nobody spoke. Five people, five reasons, and five very different starting points.

Then the lab began. The first task was simple: ask the same question to two AI tools and compare the answers. Lucía finished first and was surprised to see that her two answers disagreed. Sam found that one tool got a unit conversion wrong and the other got it right. Marcus asked about a common medication and marked every sentence he could not check. Elif noticed that one answer named a study she could not find anywhere. Hana asked about a historical event, then checked the dates in a library database and found one wrong.

By the end of the hour, the table had a list of surprises and a shared question: *If these tools can be this useful and this wrong at the same time, how do we decide when to trust them?*

That question is what this book is about.

## Where They Go From Here {.unnumbered}

You will meet one or two of them in most chapters. Each one changes over the term, and each one makes mistakes and fixes them.

| Student | Major | Starts as | Look for them in |
|---|---|---|---|
| Lucía Herrera (she) | Accounting | A daily user who values speed | Chapters 1, 5, 8, 11, 14, 15, 20 |
| Marcus Bell (he) | Nursing | A careful skeptic focused on safety | Chapters 1, 7, 9, 14, 15, 19, 21 |
| Elif Kaya (she) | Psychology | A worried user who fears losing her voice | Chapters 1, 3, 7, 9, 10, 16, 23 |
| Sam Okafor (he) | Mechanical engineering | An enthusiast who wants to automate everything | Chapters 1, 2, 4, 6, 12, 14, 17 |
| Hana Nguyen (they) | Media arts and design | An artist who opposes AI image tools | Chapters 1, 3, 13, 18, 21, 22, 23 |

None of them is the "right" one. Lucía's speed is a real strength at work; Marcus's caution protects patients; Elif's worry about her voice is a serious question; Sam's enthusiasm builds things; Hana's concern about consent is a live legal and ethical debate. The book asks you to learn from all five.

## About These Characters {.unnumbered}

**They are invented.** Lucía, Marcus, Elif, Sam and Hana are fictional composites. None of them is based on a real student, and their university is never named. Any resemblance to real people is unintended.

**Why use fictional students at all?** People remember ideas better when they meet them through a person, and a recurring cast lets this book show the same method in five different fields: business, health, social science, engineering and the arts. When Marcus checks a medication leaflet and Sam checks a unit conversion, you see that the AI Work Loop is the same habit in very different work.

**What they are not.** The characters are never used as evidence. When they meet a fact, a study or a case, it is cited like any other claim in this book. When they look at an AI output, the example is labeled either as a constructed teaching example or with the real model name and date. Their stories are teaching tools; the research in this book is real.

**How they were made.** The characters were drafted with AI assistance as part of the writing process described in "How This Book Was Written," and the author chose and approved them. Their details are kept in a single "story bible" so they stay consistent from chapter to chapter.

If one of them reminds you of yourself, that is the point. If none of them does, notice what your own starting point is. Chapter 1 asks you to write it down.
